newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Menem defiant in face of blackout protest.
newsitem.headline: Menem defiant in face of blackout protest.

text.p: President Carlos Menem remained defiant on Friday after much of Argentina was plunged into darkness by a protest blackout accompanied by clanging pots and pans and blaring car horns.
The political parties who called the five-minute blackout at 8 p.m. on Thursday said it was a "massive" success that galvanised opposition to the Peronist government.

But Menem, quoting data saying only 22 percent of homes switched off their lights, asked: "After the blackout, at 8:06, did anything change? Nothing will change and why should it? To take us back to an ignominious past?"

The Peronist leader won a second term in May 1995 with half the vote but his popularity has plunged to its lowest since 1989 in opinion polls. He told a local radio: "I don't feel abandoned, I'm not so poor of spirit. I feel stronger than ever after what happened last night, which has been blown up. I flew over the city in a helicopter last night and it was not as dark as the media said."

Clarin newspaper called the blackout "the longest five minutes in seven years" of Menem rule and television showed darkened cities across Argentina with people banging pots and pans and blasting car horns and sirens.
The Radical Party and centre-left Frepaso called for the blackout to protest against 17.1 percent unemployment and austerity measures including family allowance cuts and tax hikes.

"We feel that we articulated opposition. Nobody can offer miracles but we hope the government understands that it must correct its economic policy," Sen. Graciela Fernandez Mejide of the Frepaso said.

"By turning off the light people sent the government and opposition messages. They told the government they are fed up and need deep changes. They told us they will follow us if we continue this action," Radical leader Rodolfo Terragno said.
Menem will have little respite before a 36-hour general strike on Sept. 26, the second in two months led by the main CGT labour federation, which used to be his close ally.

"The strike is unmovable, there is no negotiating and no contact with government to suspend it," said CGT chief Rodolfo Daer. "There is no margin for lifting it unless conditions are given for the people's unhappiness and anguish to disappear."
But Menem responded: "They can hold 1,001 strikes but if they think they'll weaken me they can forget it. This Argentina that is at last attracting capital and torrents of investment won't change."
